title: Prisioner safety increased since Orangeville police station death, inquest hears
article: The Orangeville Police Service (OPS) has established various safeguards to ensure prisoner safety, a coroner's inquest into the death of Adam Sprague has heard.
Sprague, who was arrested for public intoxication, died of an oxycodone overdose while in a holding cell at the C Line police station early in the morning of Nov. 11, 2010.
The inquest examining why Sprague died in police custody began hearing testimony on Wednesday (Oct. 16).
Const. Jon Kennedy, the officer who arrested Sprague, said the gaps in protocol have been filled since his death. Previously, prisoners were checked every half hour.
"It has since changed to every 15 minutes with observations logged," Kennedy said.
Before Sprague's death, special constables were infrequently called to guard the cells.
"Now we've almost mandated that special constables be called out," said Const. Rick Romaniuk, who transported Sprague to the police station. "I don't know how much more you can improve on that."
Romaniuk, who occasionally serves as an acting sergeant, said he has a move aggressive approach to ensuring a prisoner's safety. If a person in custody wasn't moving, Romaniuk investigates.
"I wake them up. I get some sort of verbal acknowledgment," Romaniuk said.
Hiring a special constable to monitor cells is also a given for Romaniuk. In 2010, special constables were called in "more than once a week" to monitor cells.
"Management did not ever have a problem with that," Romaniuk said.
Although on call, a special constable takes about a half hour to arrive.
"I would assume the role of monitoring," Romaniuk said.
A special constable was not called the night of Sprague's death, and the prisoner was never physically checked on.
As well, cries for help from the holding cell area from another man were not answered that night.
Kevin Gale, who was arrested the same night as Sprague, told the inquest he was having a conversation with Sprague between their two cells.
"He was very upset that he wasn't told why he was arrested," Gale said. "He made a reference to he wasn't feeling all that good."
Throughout the night, Gale, who was in need of medication, said he caused a commotion by jumping and screaming to get police attention.
"I was trying to get my puffer," he said.
Gale recalled asking Sprague how he was able to sleep through his attempts to get police to answer his calls, but the man didn't answer.
"No one came into check on me. They should check," Gale said. "You shouldn't be left in a cell to rot."
Gale testified he remembered hearing an unusual gurgling noise coming from Sprague's cell.
"It sounded like he had something in his mouth," Gale said.
Cathy Clarence, who was also in a holding cell that night, told the inquest she could hear "really bad gurgling" coming from Sprague's cell.
"I heard him choking," she said.
Clarence added she could hear constant cries of "help me" coming from Sprague's cell. Gale doesn't recall Sprague call for help.
"I still heave nightmares of him screaming," Clarence said.
Ian Johnston, the lawyer representing the Orangeville Police Service at the inquest, said video surveillance of the holding cells doesn't show Sprague calling for help.
"We were all screaming. I was screaming. It would show that," Clarence replied.
Both Clarence and Gale testified police never entered the holding cell area to check on prisoners or investigate why Gale was yelling.
"If the cops had checked on him he would be here today. Simple as that," Clarence said.
A five-person jury will consider evidence from the inquest's 18 witnesses and make recommendations as to how police province-wide could avoid a similar death.
"Nobody is on trial," said Dr. Jack Stanborough, who is presiding as inquest coroner.
"We're hoping some good can come out of the death of Adam Sprague," said Karen Shea, counsel to the coroner.
Unlike criminal court, jurors are allowed to question witnesses during an inquest. Following Gale's testimony, a juror asked how he was able to talk to Sprague, as a door separated their cells.
"Cell four would be through a door and around a corner, I'm not clear how a conversation would occur," the juror said.
Gale explained there was no trouble hearing from other prisoners throughout the holding cell area.
"I don't remember the door being there," he added.

The arrests of Sprague, Clarence and Gale are all connected. Clarence picked up Sprague from Gale's home to give him a ride to the LCBO. He wanted to purchase beer for a last night of partying, before going to rehab for oxycodone addiction.
"That's why I was driving him around, so he could say goodbye," Clarence said.
Sprague had previously hidden two oxycodone pills in Gale's garage. Gale told the inquest he took one pill that night.
"He wanted to straighten his life out, he wanted to start fresh the next day," Gale said.
Police were called to Gale's Lawrence Avenue home to arrest Clarence for breaching a court order. They arrived to find Clarence in the home's garage alone with Sprague at about 10:30 p.m.
"He appeared intoxicated. He was unsteady on his feet," Kennedy said.. "He had to lean against a vehicle for support."
Sprague was then arrested for public intoxication, in his friend's garage.
"I was concerned for his wellbeing," Kennedy said. "I was concerned he could walk into traffic."
Gale asked if he could close his garage door, but was never asked if he would care for Sprague.
"I took that he wasn't interested in anyone outside of his house," Kennedy said.
Romaniuk was called to transfer Sprague to the police station.
"I assisted him in the walk (to the cruiser)," Romaniuk said. "At one point he was so quiet, I turned on the interior light."

At the station, Kennedy said the reason for Sprague's arrest was delivered to the sergeant on duty. He was not asked for further details about his condition. A surveillance tape of the booking rooms shows that Sprague and Clarence were not asked about drugs they may have consumed or medical issues.
"Anything on you? Needles or anything like that?" an officer asked Sprague. "Any communicable disease we should know about?"
Around midnight, Gale called the station to see if he could pick up Sprague. Upon his arrived, Gale was arrested for breaching a ban on consuming alcohol.
"I could smell alcohol on him," said Const. Jason Moore.
While escorting Gale to a holding cell, Moore recalled seeing Sprague sitting on his cell's cement bench.
"I asked him if he was OK. He stated there was an issue with the toilet," Moore said. 'His eyes were glossy and his lips chalky."
After Gale was placed in the cell, Moore said he could hear banging and yelling. However, the noise was of no concern to police.
"He wasn't pleased he was under arrest," Moore said.
Kennedy also recalled hearing the commotion.
"It's not unusual for prisoners to bang the bars," Kennedy said.
When Romaniuk returned from to the station from patrol, he too heard banging and a muffled male voice coming from the holding cells.
"I couldn't make out what was said," Romaniuk said. "It was going on before my arriving."

At about 6 a.m. the following morning, Kevin Ewen arrived at the station to turn himself in to police for an unrelated matter. After being booked, he was taken to the cell next to Sprague. Ewen told the inquest he walked by Sprague's cell about four times that morning.
"I was thinking to myself he's awfully quiet," Ewen said, who knew Sprague through his uncle. "He appeared to be comfortable or sleeping."

About 20 minutes after entering the cell, Ewen was removed for questioning. Sprague remained in the same position as they walked by his cell. However, Ewen said he caught the attention of the officer, who looked into the cell for about five to 10 seconds.
"He kind of did one of those double takes," Ewen said.
The inquest continues at the Dufferin County Courthouse throughout the week.
